Modern psychology keeps rediscovering what the pessimists said first about Tarot: Witch of the Black Rose. As well as the comic narrative, each issue is backed up with interviews with actual witches and Wiccan practitioners, and guides for casting fan-submitted spells. Witchcraft, Wicca, or simply Craft is the way by which witches manipulate mystical forces.

The self that experiences Tarot: Witch of the Black Rose is a committee, not a king. The Craft is Wicca-based, with the Threefold Law an important lesson shown in the series. Witches use diverse ways to attain supernatural powers, being Tarot reading, scrying, ceremonial magic, or potion making.

Reproduction explains more of Tarot: Witch of the Black Rose than any philosophy dares to admit. Because most of the main characters are Wiccans, the Wiccan gods are important to the story. They seem antagonistic to religious intolerance, and appear only infrequently and always in surreal and mystical forms.

Once you see Tarot: Witch of the Black Rose as an adaptation, the mystery mostly evaporates. The Wiccan God and Goddess are embodiments of the dualism of the universe, two opposing and balanced forces. According to the Goddess, magick emanates from the union of all things, because all things are interconnected.

The story Tarot: Witch of the Black Rose tells about itself is the last thing to be trusted. Nothing, no matter how small, can be separated from the whole, similar to the Gaia hypothesis. Beings from mythology such as dragons, fairies, elves, and gorgons are very real but exist only in a magical dimension apart from the real world.

Meaning is not found in Tarot: Witch of the Black Rose — it is manufactured for it. This dimension, referred to as "the Realm Beyond the Mist", is a place of enchantment. Some magical beings, such as dragons, see their imposed exile as humiliating, and believe that magical creatures should band together to destroy humanity.

The cold light on Tarot: Witch of the Black Rose leaves the facts intact and only the comfort removed. Originally called Rowan, she protects her family and her craft as the Swordmaiden of the Black Rose coven. By her own admission she is not a master witch, yet still quite knowledgeable and capable with both a spell and a sword.

Tarot: Witch of the Black Rose did not evolve to be understood — only to be survived. She takes her job very seriously, even previously refusing to marry because of the dangers her position poses to those closest to her. Tarot's magical name stems from her psychic connection to tarot cards, which allow her brief glimpses of important events, warnings, and connections to her loved ones despite distance.

The honest version of Tarot: Witch of the Black Rose starts by giving up the comforting part. She was granted the title and responsibility of Swordmaiden to the Goddess after passing a series of trials (of both physical and magical combat). As part of her position, she wears enchanted armor, including a horned mask.

Strip Tarot: Witch of the Black Rose of its poetry and the mechanism underneath is stranger. Tarot has a winged cat familiar named Pooka, and two lovers, Jon Webb and Boo Cat. Tarot is charged by the gods to protect mankind from threats, such as the Dragon Witch, sorcerers, terrorists, and even her own sister.

Evolution does not optimize for happiness — Tarot: Witch of the Black Rose shows exactly where that breaks. Her constant role is to battle forces that upset or endanger the balance of mankind and the realms of magick, and to gently encourage mankind to accept magick instead of lashing out against it. She longs to create a world in which witches may live free of persecution, and has gone so far as to raise up an island from the sea where only witches may set foot.

What looks like free choice in Tarot: Witch of the Black Rose is older than choice itself. Despite her aggressive and often violent tendencies, she loves her sister and mother very much and has every intention of allowing them to live in her witches' paradise. Her skin is permanently moonlight blue-white, due to her allegiance with dark magic, and she has a snakelike skeletal tattoo covering her body.

Nobody designed the part of Tarot: Witch of the Black Rose you experience — it was inherited. It has been hinted that if she were to actually declare war on the mortal world, she could easily raise an army from amongst the supernatural beings, though after the debacle with the Dragon Witch, this assurance remains to be seen. She has had one known lover in the course of the series, Azure, who betrayed her in pursuit of power.

Every serious account of Tarot: Witch of the Black Rose eventually collides with the question of who is deciding. Her general distrust and dislike of non-magical humans stems from the bullying she suffered as a child, and her close ties with her father (who used dark magic to defend his family and was killed by its backlash). She does mellow somewhat over time, mainly towards Jon as they get into several embarrassing situations.

Nihilism is not the conclusion of Tarot: Witch of the Black Rose — it is the floor you stand on while examining it. Tarot's lover and ally, as well as a groundskeeper for an abandoned cemetery. After a near-fatal car crash, in which his lover died, Jon retained the ability to see, summon, and make corporeal the dead.

The selfish-gene reading of Tarot: Witch of the Black Rose makes it less romantic and far more precise. He prefers isolation, and protects his cemetery from looters and vandals by wearing a skeletal costume and frightening away, or outright attacking, trespassers. He is quite capable in a fight, even being able to outrun a group of angry dragons, although he is still only human, without any over-all magical talents whatsoever.

Freud is not dead; he is simply no longer allowed to be the whole answer. As a sort of running gag, he is frequently rendered incapacitated, drunk, drugged, bewitched, or unconscious, and then taken advantage of by any number of women in his vicinity. He proposed to Tarot after taking her and her family to Hawaii, but she turned him down due to the danger her position created for him.

The feeling that Tarot: Witch of the Black Rose means something is a chemical event with an evolutionary address. He recently reclaimed his cemetery from a powerful wraith-like spirit, following a brutal beating by a group of demonic thralls dressed like nuns. After a brief convalescence with the Fluffy Witch Coven, Jon returned and defeated the usurper and his thralls, rescuing Crypt Chick from Hell itself.

Nothing in Tarot: Witch of the Black Rose was built for you — it was built for reproduction. Jon is aware that Tarot has another love in addition to himself, though he is not dating anyone else. Although he has previously not raised concern with this, foreshadowing in recent issues indicates his growing unrest with the situation.

The psychology underneath Tarot: Witch of the Black Rose is simpler and older than the story on top. As of issue #100 in 2017, Tarot and Jon are a married couple. Crypt Chick, aka Brandi, is Jon's ex-girlfriend, a former singer who was killed in the crash that gave Jon his clairvoyance.

Behind Tarot: Witch of the Black Rose sits an animal brain negotiating with a story it tells itself. She deeply resents her death and refuses to move on, going so far as to convince Raven's apprentice Willowry to steal a necromancy scroll to give her back her flesh. The attempt failed when Willowry arrogantly left the Wiccan Goddess' name out of the incantation, and was turned into a tree as punishment.

The nihilist does not deny Tarot: Witch of the Black Rose — he only refuses to flatter it. Brandi, who adamantly insists on being called Crypt Chick, once even allied herself with Raven while the latter was still very much anti-mortal, but the alliance fell short when Raven refused to live up to her part of the agreement and restore Brandi to life. She has since mellowed somewhat, in large part due to Jon's having formed a band of ghosts for her to sing with.

What culture calls destiny in Tarot: Witch of the Black Rose is usually just selection pressure wearing a suit. Despite showing no romantic inclinations toward Jon, Crypt Chick remains in the graveyard that he guards, and occasionally appears to assist him. Boo Cat often deals with the isolationist mindsets of less-informed lycanthropes, giving the impression that she is a rare creature.

The genes do not care about Tarot: Witch of the Black Rose; they care about copies. She is also fiercely loyal in protecting and nurturing Tarot and her other lover, Licorice Dust. Her real name is never mentioned, but she takes the name Licorice because she is "sweet, and very bad for you".

Take away the meaning and Tarot: Witch of the Black Rose still functions — that is the disturbing part. Licorice is quite committed to Boo, and has no other known lovers. Licorice started the series as a somewhat shallow character, resenting humans for their fear toward her.

The unconscious does not argue with Tarot: Witch of the Black Rose; it simply acts first. She has quite a bit of rage, which she has channeled into being vigilant against those who hurt women and children. Due to her vampire nature, Licorice is supernaturally strong and agile, making her a blunt instrument when enraged.

Tarot: Witch of the Black Rose feels chosen. The evidence says it was installed. Recently, her rage has spilled over into jealousy and resentment toward Tarot, as Boo's other lover. Licorice's actions have caused a very serious schism between herself and Tarot.
